pages.title: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
INTRODUCTION

The Conversation That Runs the World

Every political move is a scored conversation. Most players never check the score.

Every political career lives and dies in conversation.

Not in policy. Not in polling. Not in the war room at midnight or the debate stage under lights. In conversation. One person in a room with another person — or with a camera, which is just a thousand conversations happening simultaneously — and three scores running underneath every word spoken, every pause held, every question answered or deflected or redirected.

Profit. Love. Tax.

These three scores determine whether a candidate survives a debate attack or collapses under it. Whether a voter leaves a town hall feeling seen or feeling managed. Whether a donor writes the check or decides to wait and see. Whether an advisor's counsel is heard or quietly ignored. Whether the press conference ends the story or feeds it for another week.

Most political professionals understand power. They understand messaging, opposition research, ground game, polling margins, earned media cycles. They do not understand conversation scoring. They study what was said. The scorer watches what moved.

◆

This book applies the PLT Framework — Profit, Love, Tax — to the political arena in full. It teaches you to read every person in that arena: the Candidate, the Voter, the Donor, the Opponent, the Media, the Advisor, the Family. It teaches you to score the conversations between them in real time. And it gives you the nine moves — the executable doctrine that a scorer runs when the score turns in the wrong direction.

Political conversations are the highest-stakes conversations on earth. The scores running underneath them shape legislation, careers, movements, and history. The scorer who can see those movements in real time — in a debate exchange, in a constituent meeting, in a press gaggle, in a donor call, in a kitchen table conversation the candidate never attends — that scorer operates at a level most political professionals do not know exists.

This book creates that scorer.

pages.title: PART ONE
pages.html:
PART ONE

The Political Arena

Why political conversations are the hardest conversations to score — and why they must be

pages.title: CHAPTER 1
pages.html:
CHAPTER 1

The Transaction Nobody Sees

Every political interaction is a transaction.

The town hall looks like a candidate taking questions. What it actually is: a scored exchange between a politician running a Profit-maintenance play and a room full of voters running Love-deficit tests. The voters are not asking questions because they want information. They are asking questions to see how the candidate handles the question. The question is not the point. The handling is the point.

The debate looks like a policy argument. What it actually is: a live scoring event where Profit shifts on every exchange, Love accounts build and drain across the entire viewing audience simultaneously, and Tax accrues to every evasion, every stumble, every moment the candidate chose positioning over truth. The audience scores in real time. The candidate rarely knows the score until a poll surfaces three days later.

The donor meeting looks like a fundraising conversation. What it actually is: the most explicit Profit negotiation in politics. The donor holds money. The candidate holds access and influence. Both parties are negotiating the terms of an exchange that neither will ever fully articulate out loud. The Love account between them determines whether this negotiation produces a check or produces a promise to think about it.

The press conference looks like information delivery. What it actually is: a high-Tax environment where every line creates obligation, every hedge creates suspicion, and every evasion becomes the story rather than the substance.

◆

The political arena is the most complex scoring environment in existence because all five characters — Candidate, Voter, Donor, Opponent, Media — are running their own scores simultaneously, often in the same room, often in direct conflict with each other. The move that builds Profit with the donor burns Love with the voter in the back row. The move that neutralizes the opponent gives the media a better attack angle. The Honest Strike that builds Love with the press costs Tax in the caucus.

The scorer does not simplify this complexity. The scorer maps it. And operates inside it without losing the thread.

pages.title: CHAPTER 2
pages.html:
CHAPTER 2

Why Political Careers Collapse

Every political career that collapses collapses for one of three reasons.

The Profit position became untenable. The candidate lost the frame and could not recover it. The opponent defined them before they defined themselves. The narrative became about what the candidate was running from rather than what they were running toward. Once Profit collapses in a political campaign, recovery requires a move so large and so visible that it resets the entire conversation. Most candidates make smaller moves instead — tactical corrections, messaging adjustments, rebranding efforts. Small moves on a collapsing Profit position rarely work. They confirm that the candidate is reacting, not leading.

The Love account burned. Not all at once — Love almost never burns all at once. It burns in the accumulation of moments where the candidate was seen calculating when they should have been human. The evasion that was technically defensible but felt dishonest. The scripted answer in a moment that demanded a real one. The town hall where the candidate moved through the room efficiently but did not actually listen to a single person in it. Love does not end with a scandal. It ends with the slow recognition that the person asking for trust does not fully mean it.

The Tax became unbearable. The risk of continued association exceeded the value of the relationship. Donors who decide the candidate cannot win. Advisors who start looking for other positions. Party leadership that stops returning calls. Voters who tell pollsters they might sit this one out. Tax does not announce itself. It accumulates quietly in the background until the visible support structure begins to shift — and by the time it is visible, it has been building for months.

◆

The political scorer sees these three collapses before they are visible in polling. Because every collapse is preceded by a series of small score movements that are audible in conversations — in how the candidate answers the question they did not want to answer, in how the donor pauses before saying yes, in how the press moves from reporting to investigating.

The score moves before the headline. The scorer moves before the score.

pages.title: PART TWO
pages.html:
PART TWO

The Seven Characters

Everyone in the arena. How their scores run. How to read them.

01

The Candidate

The Candidate is running the most public scoring event in existence.

Every conversation they have is observed, recorded, interpreted, and distributed. There is no private conversation for a candidate at scale — only conversations with different audience sizes. The conversation with a single voter in a diner is also a conversation with everyone who will ever see the footage. The debate exchange with an opponent is also a conversation with every undecided voter watching from a living room. The Candidate who understands this runs every conversation at two levels simultaneously: the person in front of them, and the audience that will experience it.

The Candidate's primary scoring challenge: maintaining Profit across audiences that want different things from the same conversation. The donor wants authority. The voter wants authenticity. The media wants clarity. The opponent wants exposure. These are not always compatible positions. The candidate who tries to optimize all four simultaneously usually achieves none of them cleanly.

◆

The highest-Profit Candidates are not the ones who say the most. They are the ones who control the frame of every conversation they enter. They name the issue before the opponent names it. They set the terms of the comparison. They decide what the conversation is about — and they make that decision before they walk into the room.

The highest-Love Candidates are not the most likable. They are the most honest about the things that are hard to be honest about. Voters have extremely accurate detectors for managed authenticity. The candidate who admits a mistake before being forced to, who acknowledges a limitation before an opponent exploits it, who says "I don't know" in a moment when saying "I don't know" is the harder answer — that candidate builds Love that survives the campaign.

Reading the Candidate's score: Profit — are they setting the agenda or responding to it? Love — when they answer a difficult question, does the room lean in or sit back? Tax — how many of their statements have created obligations they have not yet fulfilled?

02

The Voter

The Voter is not deciding between policies. They are deciding between people.

The research on political decision-making is consistent: voters decide with the Love account first and justify it with policy second. The candidate who wins the Love account of a voter can lose almost every policy argument with that voter and still hold their vote. The candidate who never builds the Love account loses the vote even when they are objectively correct on every issue.

The Voter's primary question in every interaction with a candidate: does this person actually see me? Not as a demographic. Not as a vote to be earned. As a person with a specific situation that this election will affect in a specific way. The voter who feels seen by a candidate defends that candidate at the dinner table. The voter who feels processed — efficiently moved through a receiving line, given a practiced answer to a genuine question — becomes the voter who "doesn't love either candidate."

◆

The Voter runs high Tax in every political interaction. They are calculating risk: what does supporting this candidate cost me? Socially. Professionally. In terms of what they might have to explain to people they respect. The candidate who can reduce the perceived Tax of support — who makes the voter feel that choosing them is the safe, reasonable, defensible choice rather than the risky or divisive one — moves votes at a scale that no messaging strategy can replicate.

Reading the Voter's score: Profit — do they believe the candidate can actually win? A voter whose candidate has no Profit position does not vote — they stay home. Love — have they told someone else about the candidate without being asked? Word-of-mouth is the purest Love signal in politics. Tax — what are they afraid the choice will cost them?

03

The Donor

The Donor is running the most explicit Profit conversation in the arena.

They have capital. The candidate needs it. That is the entire structure of the relationship before a single word is spoken. The Donor knows they have Profit. The candidate knows the Donor knows. The question every donor meeting is actually answering is: does this candidate's Profit trajectory justify the investment of my capital, and do I trust them enough to make that investment now rather than waiting for more certainty?

The second question is Love. The Donor who trusts the candidate gives early, gives at the ceiling, and brings other donors. The Donor who respects the candidate but does not fully trust them gives at the floor, gives late, and waits to see who else is in before committing their network.

◆

The Donor's Tax calculation is reputation. Every significant political donation is public. Donors know this. When they write a check for a candidate, they are accepting the Tax that comes with association — they will be identified with that candidate's wins and with their losses, their positions and their controversies. The donor meeting is not just a capital conversation. It is a reputation negotiation.

Reading the Donor's score: Profit — do they ask about the path to victory, or do they assume it? Donors who ask about the path have not decided. Donors who assume it have. Love — do they refer to the candidate by first name? The shift from last name to first name in a donor conversation is one of the most reliable Love signals in the meeting. Tax — do they ask about the opposition research before they ask about the platform?

04

The Opponent

The Opponent's entire strategy is a Tax operation.

Their goal is not to build their own Love account — though they need enough Love to remain viable. Their goal is to make the Tax of supporting the other candidate so high that their opponent's voters decide the cost is not worth it. Opposition research, negative advertising, debate attacks, earned media strategy — all of it is Tax delivery. Making the other candidate's positions, record, associations, and character feel like liabilities to anyone considering support.

The Opponent who understands PLT runs the most disciplined attack: they build their own Love first, establish their own Profit position second, and deploy Tax on the opponent only once they have enough Love to make the attack credible. An attack from a low-Love position does not land — it reads as desperate. An attack from a high-Love position reads as the truth.

◆

The Opponent is also the most important mirror for the Candidate's own score. Every attack the opponent runs successfully is a signal that a score is vulnerable. The candidate who is being attacked on their record has a Profit problem — the opponent has found a frame that is sticking. The candidate being attacked on their character has a Love problem — the attacks are finding fertile ground. The candidate being attacked on their associations has a Tax problem — the opponent is surfacing obligations that the candidate has not managed.

The scorer watches the opponent's attack lines as a diagnostic tool. Where the attacks land is where the score is weakest.

05

The Media

The Media is not covering the campaign. The Media is scoring it.

Every political journalist is running a Profit calculation on every candidate simultaneously — who is gaining, who is losing, who controls the narrative, who is being defined by the narrative versus defining it. The horse race is not a lazy journalistic habit. It is the natural output of covering a competition through a Profit lens: who is ahead, who is behind, who is making the moves that change the answer to those two questions.

The Media's Love account with a candidate is built on access and honesty. The candidate who tells a journalist something that costs them something — who acknowledges a vulnerability, who gives a real answer to a question designed to produce a managed one — builds Love with that journalist that translates into coverage with a different quality than the coverage produced by managed access and prepared answers.

◆

The Media runs the highest-Tax environment in the political arena. Every line a candidate delivers to a journalist is potentially permanent. Every evasion is recorded. Every contradiction against prior statements is archived. The Tax of a press conference is not in the questions asked — it is in the obligations created by the answers given. The candidate who leaves a press conference having said nothing has paid Tax in a different currency: they have fed the story that they have something to hide.

pages.title: PART TWO (cont. 2)
pages.html:
Reading the Media's score: Profit — are they asking about the campaign's position or the campaign's future? Position questions are historical. Future questions mean the journalist thinks the story is still developing. Love — are they giving the campaign advance notice of stories, or are they publishing without a call for comment? Tax — how many of the candidate's prior statements are they citing in current coverage?

06

The Advisor

The Advisor is running the only purely internal score in the campaign.

Their Profit is not public. It is positional — how much influence do they actually have over the decisions being made? The Advisor who is in the room when the major choices happen is running high Profit. The Advisor whose counsel is heard and then set aside is running Profit on paper and zero in practice.

The Advisor's Love account with the Candidate is the most fragile relationship in the campaign. It is built on honest counsel and destroyed by managed counsel. The Advisor who tells the Candidate what they need to hear builds Love. The Advisor who tells the Candidate what they want to hear builds access in the short term and gets replaced when the advice runs out of results.

◆

The Advisor also runs a Tax account that most campaigns underestimate: the Tax of their public association. An Advisor's past clients, positions, and controversies attach to the candidate. The opposition research that surfaces an Advisor's prior work is a Tax delivery aimed at the candidate through the Advisor's record. The Advisor who understands this manages their own public profile with the same discipline the candidate manages theirs.

The highest-value Advisor move: telling the candidate something true that the candidate does not want to hear, in a way that the candidate can actually receive. This is Move 02 — the Honest Strike — applied to the internal conversation. It is the rarest move in any campaign and the most important one.

07

The Family

The Family did not run for office.

This is the most important sentence in this chapter. The Family is in the arena because of the Candidate's decision, not their own. Their Tax burden is real and they did not choose it. Their scrutiny is total and they did not earn it. Their Love for the Candidate is the only capital they have and it is being spent by a campaign that did not ask for their permission to spend it.

The Family's presence in the campaign serves a specific Love function: it makes the Candidate human in a way no speechwriter can manufacture. The moment a candidate is seen as a spouse, a parent, a child — before they are seen as a politician — is the moment their Love account with the broadest audience moves fastest. The Family is the most powerful Love asset in the campaign.

◆

The Family is also the most significant Tax liability if the campaign is running poorly. Every family member who expresses doubt publicly. Every domestic difficulty that becomes a narrative. Every child who says something unscripted. The campaign that treats Family as a prop rather than a person creates Tax it cannot manage — because authenticity cannot be faked by people who are not actors, and voters know the difference.

The scorer watches the Family conversation for one signal above all others: does the Candidate change when they are with their family in front of an audience? The Candidate who becomes more themselves — less managed, more present — is running a genuine relationship. The Candidate who becomes more performed — who uses their family as staging — is running a Love move that the audience will eventually reject.

pages.title: PART THREE
pages.html:
PART THREE

The 9 Moves in the Arena

The same nine moves. The highest-stakes environment they have ever been run in.

The nine moves do not change between industries.

The Frame Reset runs the same way in a negotiation room and on a debate stage. The Honest Strike builds Love the same way in a donor meeting and in a press conference. The Patience Play holds Profit the same way in a real estate offer and in a Senate hearing. What changes is the stakes, the audience, and the Tax of running each move incorrectly.

Move 01: The Frame Reset in the Arena

The Frame Reset is the most important move in political debate.

When an opponent lands an attack that is finding traction, the natural response is to defend. The Candidate who defends is accepting the opponent's frame — they are arguing about the thing the opponent named, on the ground the opponent chose. Defense on your opponent's ground is Profit surrender regardless of how good the defense is.

The Frame Reset abandons the defense entirely. It does not dispute the attack. It moves the conversation to a different category — one the Candidate controls.

◆

Opponent: "My opponent voted against the infrastructure bill three times."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 52 ▼ 12|LOVE 64 —|TAX 42 ▲ 10

MOVE ATTACK — PROFIT AND TAX IMPACT

The opponent has placed a voting record on the record. Profit drops for the Candidate because they are now in a reactive position. Tax builds because the accusation creates an obligation to respond.

Candidate: "What my opponent calls voting against a bill, voters call reading what's in it. The question for this district is not how many times I voted — the question is what actually got built. I'll take that record anywhere."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 ▲ 20|LOVE 66 ▲ 2|TAX 26 ▼ 16

MOVE FRAME RESET — MOVE 01

The Candidate did not dispute the vote count. They reframed the vote count as evidence of diligence rather than obstruction. Profit recovers significantly because the Candidate has moved from defense to counterattack — and their counterattack is on ground they control. Tax drops because the obligation to defend the votes has been converted into a challenge to the opponent's framing.

Move 02: The Honest Strike in the Arena

The Honest Strike in politics is the rarest and most powerful move available.

Political professionals are trained to minimize, deflect, and reframe every vulnerability. The Honest Strike does the opposite — it names the vulnerability before the opponent can name it, owns it completely, and then moves forward. This move is so counter-intuitive to campaign instinct that most candidates never run it. The candidates who do run it almost always build more Love in that single moment than they built in the preceding month of campaigning.

◆

Candidate at town hall: "Before we get into my position on the budget — I want to say something about my vote on the education amendment last year. I got that one wrong. I had incomplete information and I voted on it too quickly. Here is what I've learned since then and here is where I stand now."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 68 ▲ 4|LOVE 92 ▲ 22|TAX 28 ▼ 8

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02

Love builds 22 points — the single largest score movement in this book. The Candidate admitted a mistake before being asked to. In a political environment where every admission is treated as a liability, voluntary admission reads as courage. It disarms the opponent who was holding that vote as an attack. It disarms the media who was waiting for the moment to ask about it. And it builds a Love account with voters that is almost impossible to break — because they now believe the Candidate will tell them the truth even when it costs something.

Move 03: The Intelligence Transfer in the Arena

In the political arena, Intelligence Transfer is how advisors build Profit with candidates and how candidates build Profit with voters.

The Advisor who brings the Candidate information they did not have — polling data the campaign has not seen, an opposition move the research team caught early, a community concern that has not surfaced in the public conversation yet — is running Move 03. They are making the Candidate more capable than they would have been without the conversation. That is the highest-value move an Advisor can run.

The Candidate who shares relevant information with a voter before the voter knew to ask for it is running the same move in the opposite direction. The town hall moment where the Candidate says "I want to tell you something about how this policy will actually affect your district — not the talking points, the actual mechanism" — that is Intelligence Transfer. It builds Profit because the Candidate has demonstrated they know more than the voter expected. It builds Love because they shared it.

Move 04: The Evidence Mirror in the Arena

The Evidence Mirror in politics is the debate move that ends arguments.

The candidate who argues against an opponent's position gives the opponent something to argue back against. The candidate who mirrors the evidence back to the audience — and lets the audience reach the conclusion — ends the argument without creating a counterargument.

◆

Candidate, in debate: "I don't need to tell you what my opponent's record shows. The numbers are public. The votes are on record. I'd invite every voter in this room to look up the last six votes cast on housing legislation and tell me what they see."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 78 ▲ 10|LOVE 68 ▲ 6|TAX 18 ▼ 12

MOVE EVIDENCE MIRROR — MOVE 04

The Candidate transferred the conclusion to the audience. They did not make the argument — they made the invitation. Tax drops sharply because the Candidate has created no obligation: they have not claimed anything that can be disputed, they have simply pointed at publicly available evidence. Profit builds because they have positioned themselves as the candidate who trusts the audience's intelligence. Love builds because that trust is felt.

Move 05: The Ownership Move in the Arena

The Ownership Move is the move that saves political careers.

Political scandals rarely end careers by themselves. The cover-up ends the career. The management of the story ends the career. The series of increasingly implausible denials ends the career. The scandal is the Tax. The management of the scandal is the Love account that either survives or drains.

The Candidate who runs Move 05 at the first credible sign of a vulnerability — who owns the mistake before it becomes a story, before the investigation, before the opposition research surfaces it — pays Tax in the short term and builds the Love account that carries them through. The Candidate who waits until the story is unavoidable has paid the Tax without getting the Love.

◆

Candidate, press conference: "I made a decision about campaign finance reporting that I believed was compliant. I have since learned it was not. Here is what happened, here is what we are doing to correct it, and here is what I should have done differently."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 ▼ 4|LOVE 82 ▲ 18|TAX 36 ▲ 12

MOVE OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVE 05

Tax builds because the Candidate has accepted responsibility — that debt is real. Profit drops slightly because they have acknowledged a vulnerability. But Love builds 18 points because the move was complete, unqualified, and proactive. The candidate who pays Tax willingly to build Love is running the correct long-term score calculation. The Tax is short-term. The Love is permanent.

Moves 06, 07, 08, 09 in the Arena

Move 06 — The Pressure Reveal — is the move that wins debates.

The Candidate who can identify the external pressure shaping their opponent's position — and name it in the room — changes the entire conversation. "My opponent's position on this issue shifted immediately after their largest donor category changed. I'd ask voters to look at that timing." That is Move 06 run at full expression in a political debate. The scorer identifies the pressure. The scorer names it.

◆

Move 07 — Family Inclusion — is the move most campaigns run incorrectly.

Campaigns use family as backdrop. The scorer uses family as relationship evidence. The Candidate who allows their family to be genuinely present — not scripted, not positioned, not used — is running the most powerful Love move in the campaign. A candidate's family who speaks about them without a prepared line is worth more Love than any advertisement the campaign will ever produce.

◆

Move 08 — The Patience Play — is the most underused move in political press management.

pages.title: PART THREE (cont. 2)
pages.html:
The candidate who does not fill every silence in a press conference gives the media less to build on, not more. The pause that allows a more precise answer — rather than the immediate answer that commits to a position before the candidate has fully thought it through — is the Patience Play. The candidate who can sit in the discomfort of a beat of silence in front of cameras is running a Profit position most politicians never develop.

◆

Move 09 — The Path Forward — is the move that ends crises.

When a political conversation stalls — when a scandal is dominating, when polling has collapsed, when the narrative has become about survival rather than vision — the candidate who creates a clear, specific, executable next step moves the conversation forward. Not a pivot. Not a reframe. A path. "Here is what I am going to do next week, specifically, and here is why it matters for this district." People follow the person who creates movement. In politics, movement is survival.

pages.title: PART FOUR
pages.html:
PART FOUR

The Conversations

Every pairing in the arena. Scored in real time.

CANDIDATE / VOTER

The Town Hall

Where elections are actually won and lost

Senator Marcus Webb is at a town hall in a district he won by 4 points four years ago. A teacher named Diane stands up.

◆

Diane: "I have thirty-two kids in my class. The funding bill you supported cut my supply budget by 40 percent. My question is — do you actually know what that means for a classroom?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 52 ▼ 12|LOVE 56 —|TAX 46 ▲ 10

MOVE ACCOUNTABILITY CHALLENGE — PROFIT AND TAX IMPACT

Diane has run a precision attack: a personal, specific, documented grievance. Profit drops because the Senator is now in a reactive position on specific ground the voter controls. Tax builds because a direct "do you know what that means" creates an obligation to demonstrate that he does.

Webb: "Thirty-two kids. I want to make sure I'm hearing that. What grade?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 54 ▲ 2|LOVE 66 ▲ 10|TAX 38 ▼ 8

MOVE PATIENCE PLAY + ATTENTION SIGNAL — MOVES 08 & 06

Webb did not defend the vote. He asked a question that extended the human moment. Love builds 10 points because Diane — and everyone watching — just saw a politician slow down and ask for more context instead of rushing to justify themselves. Tax drops because the immediate obligation to defend has been paused.

Diane: "Fourth grade."

Webb: "I'm going to tell you something I should have said publicly months ago. The modeling we used for that bill had a flaw in the per-district calculation. I signed on before we caught it. That's on me. Here is the correction I've already filed and here is what I need from you to make sure we get this right."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 66 ▲ 12|LOVE 90 ▲ 24|TAX 32 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVES 02 & 05

Two moves run simultaneously. The Honest Strike named the error before the opponent could. The Ownership Move claimed it completely and without qualification. Love builds 24 points — the largest single movement in this book. Webb just converted a hostile voter into a potential advocate by doing the one thing she did not expect: telling her the truth.

CANDIDATE / DONOR

The Fundraiser Call

Where capital is committed or withheld

Candidate Elena Reyes is on a call with major donor Richard Ashworth. She is in a competitive primary. The call is fifteen minutes.

◆

Ashworth: "Tell me why you can actually win this."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 60 —|LOVE 58 —|TAX 36 ▲ 8

MOVE VIABILITY TEST — TAX INTRODUCTION

This is not a friendly question. It is a Profit examination. Ashworth is establishing whether Elena's Profit trajectory justifies his capital and reputation. Tax builds because Elena must now either prove viability or watch Ashworth's interest begin to drain.

Reyes: "I'm not going to tell you why I can win. I'm going to show you the three data points our internal polling is seeing that nobody else has published yet and let you tell me what you see."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 16|LOVE 68 ▲ 10|TAX 24 ▼ 12

MOVE EVIDENCE MIRROR + INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVES 04 & 03

Elena ran two moves simultaneously. She declined to give the expected pitch — which Ashworth has heard a hundred times — and instead ran Intelligence Transfer followed by Evidence Mirror. Profit builds because she has demonstrated she has information the donor does not have. Love builds because she treated him as a partner in the analysis rather than a target of the pitch. Tax drops because she has removed the obligation to sell — instead she is inviting a shared conclusion.

Ashworth: "Where are you on the western counties?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 80 ▲ 4|LOVE 70 ▲ 2|TAX 20 ▼ 4

MOVE ENGAGEMENT — DONOR IS DECIDING

Ashworth asked a follow-up question about a specific geography. He is no longer testing viability — he is doing due diligence. The shift from viability question to specific question is the clearest Profit signal in a donor conversation. Elena is likely to get the check.

CANDIDATE / MEDIA

The Press Conference

Where every line creates permanent obligation

Candidate Jordan Hayes is at a press conference three days after an opposition research drop about a past business relationship.

◆

Reporter: "The documents show payments from a company later investigated for fraud. Can you explain your relationship with them?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 50 ▼ 14|LOVE 56 —|TAX 52 ▲ 12

MOVE ACCOUNTABILITY ATTACK — CRITICAL TAX

The Tax position is critical. The reporter has connected the candidate to a fraud investigation through documentation. This is not a rumor — it is a sourced question. How this is answered in the next thirty seconds determines whether this story runs for one day or ten.

Hayes: "I worked with that company on a logistics contract in 2018. The contract was completed. At no point was I aware of or involved in the practices that became the subject of their investigation. I'm going to be direct: if there are documents that suggest otherwise, I want to see them, and I'll address every specific on the record. What else do you have?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 ▲ 14|LOVE 72 ▲ 16|TAX 36 ▼ 16

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 02 & 09

Hayes did four things simultaneously: stated the facts cleanly, denied involvement without qualifying the denial, invited further documentation rather than avoiding it, and moved the conversation forward with a direct question. Profit recovers because Hayes is no longer in a defensive posture. Love builds because the lack of hedging reads as honesty. Tax drops significantly because Hayes has removed the story's legs — there is no more to reveal because they just offered to address everything.

CANDIDATE / OPPONENT

The Debate

The highest-stakes scored conversation in the political world

Two candidates in the final debate before a primary election. Twelve million viewers. Three weeks to election day.

◆

Opponent: "My opponent has been in office for eight years. Name one thing — one specific, measurable thing — that has changed for working families in this district because of their work."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 46 ▼ 16|LOVE 62 —|TAX 50 ▲ 12

MOVE LEGACY ATTACK — PROFIT CRITICAL

This is one of the most sophisticated attacks in political debate: it does not dispute a position, it disputes a record. Profit drops critically. The Candidate must now either defend eight years of work under attack conditions, or reframe the question entirely. Defense answers produce weak responses. A Frame Reset produces a different conversation.

Candidate: "I'm glad you asked that in front of twelve million people. Because that question has a real answer, and you know it. The Meridian Workforce Act — which passed with my sponsorship — has placed 4,200 people in jobs paying 40 percent above what they were earning before. Those people have names. I've been in their kitchens. I know what changed. The question I'd ask the audience is: what has changed in your district because of my opponent's work? Take your time."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 78 ▲ 32|LOVE 70 ▲ 8|TAX 24 ▼ 26

MOVE FRAME RESET + EVIDENCE MIRROR + PATIENCE PLAY — MOVES 01, 04, 08

Three moves in one response. The Frame Reset converted "name one thing" from an attack into an opportunity by having a specific answer ready. The Evidence Mirror transferred the conclusion to the audience ("you tell me what changed"). The Patience Play at the end — "take your time" — applied the opponent's original attack format back at the opponent with precision. Profit makes its largest single recovery in this book: 32 points. The candidate won this debate exchange.

ADVISOR / CANDIDATE

The Campaign Room

Where the most important conversations never become public

Three weeks before election day. Internal polling is down 6 points from last month. Campaign manager Toni is in the candidate's office alone with them.

◆

Toni: "I need to tell you something that's going to be hard to hear, and I need you to actually hear it."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 62 —|LOVE 70 ▲ 4|TAX 34 ▲ 8

MOVE HONEST STRIKE SETUP — LOVE AND TAX SIGNAL

Toni is prefacing the Honest Strike. The preface itself is a Love move — she is giving the candidate a moment to prepare rather than landing the difficult truth without warning. Tax builds because the candidate now knows something significant is coming.

Candidate: "Say it."

pages.title: PART FOUR (cont. 2)
pages.html:
Toni: "The authenticity problem is real. Voters are telling our focus groups that they like your positions but they don't believe you believe them. That's not a messaging problem. That's a presence problem. And the only move that fixes it is the one you've been avoiding — the personal story. The real one. Not the version we have on the website."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 66 ▲ 4|LOVE 78 ▲ 8|TAX 38 ▲ 4

MOVE HONEST STRIKE — MOVE 02 AT HIGHEST EXPRESSION

Toni ran the Honest Strike in its most complete form: specific, unqualified, and with a solution attached. Love builds because this is exactly the conversation a candidate needs and almost never gets from their inner circle. Profit builds because the diagnosis is precise. Tax builds because the candidate now has an obligation — they must decide whether to run the move Toni is suggesting or not.

Candidate: "Which story."

Toni: "The one about your father. The real version, not the campaign version. Voters can tell the difference. Run it in the next town hall, unrehearsed, and let the room respond."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 ▲ 6|LOVE 80 ▲ 2|TAX 30 ▼ 8

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

Toni gave the candidate a specific, executable next step. Not a strategy. A move. Run this story, in this format, in this venue. Tax drops because the path is clear. This is the advisor running the full Scorer system in a single conversation: Honest Strike to diagnose, Path Forward to execute.

CANDIDATE / FAMILY

Before the Debate

The conversation the world never sees

Two hours before the most important debate of the campaign. The candidate is at home. Their spouse, Carmen, is in the kitchen.

◆

Carmen: "You're performing."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 58 ▼ 6|LOVE 72 —|TAX 36 ▲ 8

MOVE FAMILY HONEST STRIKE — UNMATCHABLE LOVE

The family member just ran Move 02 from the only position that makes it completely undeniable: they love the candidate and have nothing to gain by saying it. Profit drops because the candidate has been called out on a vulnerability they cannot strategically manage. Tax builds because the observation creates an obligation to respond honestly.

Candidate: "I know."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 60 ▲ 2|LOVE 82 ▲ 10|TAX 28 ▼ 8

MOVE OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVE 05 IN ITS SIMPLEST FORM

Two words. No defense. No qualification. No explanation. "I know" is the Ownership Move at its most essential. Love builds 10 points because Carmen just saw the person she married instead of the candidate she has been watching for months. Tax drops because the managed position has been abandoned. This conversation — two hours before the debate — is the one that matters most.

Carmen: "Just talk to them. Not at them."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 ▲ 4|LOVE 86 ▲ 4|TAX 22 ▼ 6

MOVE PATH FORWARD — MOVE 09

Carmen gave the candidate the only piece of debate advice that actually matters. Not a talking point. Not a strategy. A move. The debate went differently because of this conversation. The scorer always tracks the family conversation because it is the one that shapes everything that follows.

pages.title: PART FIVE
pages.html:
PART FIVE

The Drills

Score the political move before reading the answer.

Political conversations are the hardest to score because the stakes distort the signals. Everything feels more urgent. Every pause feels more significant. The discipline is to score what actually moved — not what felt dramatic.

DRILL 01

"I've dedicated my life to public service."

Is this a Profit move, Love move, or Tax move? For whom?

ANSWER P −4 · L +2 · T +6

Candidate Tax +6. This is one of the most Tax-heavy lines in political conversation — not because it is false, but because it creates a standard the candidate must now consistently meet. Any subsequent behavior that contradicts "dedicated my life to public service" will be held against this line specifically. Love builds slightly because the statement signals commitment. Profit drops because "dedicated my life" is a defensive framing — it is justifying rather than leading.

DRILL 02

"My opponent will say anything to get elected."

Score this attack. Who does it help and who does it hurt?

ANSWER P Opponent −4 · L +0 · T +8

Opponent Tax +8, Profit −4. This attack is one of the weakest in political vocabulary because it is non-specific and applies to every candidate including the one saying it. Tax builds because the line creates an obligation the opponent cannot fulfill — "anything" is a category, not a charge. The attack is also a Love move in reverse: it reads as desperate, which signals that the candidate running it is behind on the score.

DRILL 03

"I hear you. And I want to make sure I understand what you're describing before I respond."

Score this town hall line. Which moves are being run?

ANSWER P +4 · L +12 · T −8

Love +12, Profit +4, Tax −8. Moves 08 and 06 simultaneously. The candidate is running the Patience Play ("before I respond") and signaling a Pressure Reveal ("I want to make sure I understand"). Love builds significantly because the voter just heard a politician slow down instead of pivot. Tax drops because the pause creates space for a more accurate response, reducing the obligation that comes with an incomplete answer.

DRILL 04

"That's a great question."

Score this debate opener. What is actually happening?

ANSWER P −6 · L −4 · T +8

Candidate Profit −6, Love −4, Tax +8. One of the most reliably damaging lines in political conversation. It signals that the candidate was not listening to the question — they were waiting for their turn to speak. Voters know this immediately. Tax builds because the line creates an expectation of a real answer that the filler phrase suggests may not come. The candidate has spent Love and Profit to buy three seconds. The trade is never worth it.

DRILL 05

"I was wrong about that vote. I've thought about it a lot and I would vote differently today."

Score this admission. What happens to the Love account?

ANSWER P +4 · L +20 · T +6

Love +20. The largest Love movement available in political conversation. The Ownership Move run in full. Tax builds because the admission creates accountability — the candidate has now stated publicly what they would do differently, which creates a new standard. Profit builds slightly because the admission is proactive — the candidate chose when and how to surface this, which is Profit control. The Love gain dominates all other movements.

DRILL 06

"I'll have my team look into that and get back to you."

Score this response to a constituent question at a town hall.

ANSWER P −8 · L −8 · T +12

Tax +12. The political equivalent of "let me see what I can do." It creates an obligation with no timeline, no accountability mechanism, and no evidence that the candidate has any intention of following through. Voters have heard this line so many times it has become the audible signal that they are being managed rather than heard. Both Profit and Love drop because the response reveals that the candidate did not know the answer and chose to hide that rather than admit it.

DRILL 07

"The people of this district deserve better than what Washington has given them."

Is this a high-Profit line? Why or why not?

ANSWER P −4 · L +2 · T −4

Profit −4. This is a frame move that appears to be Profit but is actually Profit neutral at best. It establishes an adversarial relationship with Washington — but the candidate is running to be part of Washington. The line creates a frame the candidate will have to exit the moment they win. Love ticks up slightly because it signals alignment with voter frustration. But sophisticated voters hear the contradiction. The scorer marks this as a low-Profit line masquerading as a populist move.

DRILL 08

"I've always believed that this community's best days are ahead."

Score this closing statement line. What does it actually do?

ANSWER P 0 · L 0 · T +4

Tax +4. Nothing else moves. This line is the political equivalent of white noise — it creates mild obligation (the candidate has staked a position on the community's future) with no Profit gain and no Love movement because it is expected, generic, and indistinguishable from every other candidate's closing statement. The scorer marks any line that produces no Profit and no Love movement as Tax — it was said, it created obligation, and it built nothing in return.

pages.title: PART SIX
pages.html:
PART SIX

The Field Guide

What to watch. What it means. What to do. Every political situation.

At The Debate

THE OPPONENT LANDS AN UNEXPECTED ATTACK

WATCH The candidate pauses longer than normal before responding.

MEANS The candidate did not have a prepared response for this specific attack. They are calculating in real time.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 01 — Frame Reset. Do not defend the specific claim. Move the ground the claim is standing on. A reframe takes the same time as a defense and produces ten times the Profit.

THE OPPONENT REFUSES TO ANSWER A DIRECT QUESTION

WATCH The opponent pivots to a pre-prepared line after a question about their record.

MEANS The opponent has a vulnerability on this topic they are managing. The pivot is a Tax signal.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 04 — Evidence Mirror. "I notice my opponent didn't answer that question. I'd invite voters to look at the record themselves." Point at the avoidance. Let the audience score it.

THE MODERATOR ASKS A QUESTION YOU ARE NOT PREPARED FOR

WATCH The candidate's opening word is "look" or "listen" before the answer.

MEANS The candidate is buying time with a setup word. Voters register this even when they cannot name it.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 08 — the Patience Play. A beat of genuine silence followed by a real answer is always stronger than an immediate answer that is partially formed.

At The Town Hall

A VOTER CHALLENGES A SPECIFIC VOTE OR DECISION

WATCH The voter's voice is calm but their question is specific and documented.

MEANS This is a prepared challenge. The voter came with this question. They have researched it. A general defense will not satisfy them.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 06 — Pressure Reveal. Ask a follow-up question before responding. "Can you tell me a bit more about how this affected you directly?" Specificity earns specificity.

THE ROOM'S ENERGY DROPS DURING AN ANSWER

WATCH Audience members begin looking at phones or shifting in seats mid-response.

MEANS The answer has gone too long or too technical. The Love account is draining in real time.

YOUR MOVE Stop the answer where it is. Run Move 09 — the Path Forward. Give a one-sentence conclusion and ask a question back to the room. Movement restores attention.

A VOTER ASKS A QUESTION YOU GENUINELY DO NOT KNOW THE ANSWER TO

WATCH The candidate begins an answer with confident language but the substance is thin.

MEANS The candidate is generating plausible-sounding content without genuine knowledge. Voters detect this.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 02 — the Honest Strike. "I don't have a specific answer to that right now and I won't pretend I do. Here is what I do know, and here is how I will find the rest." Three sentences. Maximum Love gain from minimum content.

At The Press Conference

A REPORTER ASKS ABOUT A DOCUMENT OR STATEMENT YOU DID NOT EXPECT

WATCH The candidate asks the reporter to repeat the question.

MEANS The candidate is buying time and hoping the re-ask gives them more information about what the reporter actually has.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 05 — Ownership Move if there is anything to own. Run Move 03 — Intelligence Transfer if you have information the reporter does not. Never buy time visibly. The camera catches it.

MULTIPLE REPORTERS ARE ASKING THE SAME QUESTION IN DIFFERENT FORMS

WATCH The press conference has developed a consensus focus on a single topic.

MEANS The room has decided this topic is the story. Everything else is secondary.

YOUR MOVE Address it directly, completely, and once. Then create movement with Move 09: "Here is what I will be focused on this week and why it matters." Force the story to compete with a path forward.

At The Donor Meeting

THE DONOR ASKS ABOUT INTERNAL POLLING NUMBERS

WATCH The donor is asking for data you have not released publicly.

MEANS This is a viability test. The donor is determining whether the investment is sound.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 03 — Intelligence Transfer. Share what you have. Donors who receive real intelligence before it is public become advocates, not just funders. The donor who sees your internal polling alongside your public message knows they are being treated as a partner.

THE DONOR MENTIONS THEY ARE ALSO TALKING TO OTHER CANDIDATES

WATCH The disclosure is casual but deliberate.

MEANS The donor is deploying a competing offer signal to improve their own Profit position in the conversation.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 08 — the Patience Play. Do not compete for the donor. Make the case for your campaign on its own terms and let the comparison resolve itself. The candidate who chases a donor has just transferred Profit to the donor.

The vote is not the end of the score.

Every vote earned in an election was preceded by a hundred scored conversations — in town halls, in donor meetings, in press gaggles, at kitchen tables, in debate exchanges, in private rooms where advisors told candidates things they did not want to hear and candidates either listened or didn't.

The candidate who wins is almost never the most qualified. They are the candidate whose scores held up longest across the highest number of conversations. The candidate who maintained Profit when the attacks came. Whose Love account was built deep enough to survive the moment it was tested. Who managed Tax before it became a crisis instead of after.

The political scorer does not watch the polls. The scorer watches the conversations that will determine what the polls say next week.

Profit. Love. Tax.

Every conversation. Every arena.

About the Author

Craig Jones is the founder of the PLT Framework and the architect of the PLT Doctrine Series. He writes under the name Little Bunny. The PLT Framework was built from direct observation of how high-stakes conversations actually work — what gets exchanged when power and trust are in the same room simultaneously, what causes positions to hold and what causes them to collapse, and what the scorer sees that everyone else in the room misses. The Scorer: Politics is the application of that doctrine to the most consequential arena on earth.
